Comment.MultiLanguageText: The position source normalised so TRUE always means PROVEN OPEN, whichever state the source is wired to prove. Both detections, the enable, the cycle count and the status code read it, so the sense question has exactly one answer in the block.
One scan on the rising edge of a debounced proven-open operation, for the cycle counter. The live half of the explicit edge construction.
The debounced proven-open state as it was last scan. The stored half of the explicit edge construction; nothing else may read it.
The fail-to preset in milliseconds, derived once from the operator-facing seconds figure. BOTH fail-to timers share it, which is what makes them one setting rather than two free to drift apart.
The upstream-enable preset in milliseconds, derived once from the operator-facing seconds figure.

AttributeList.Text: CONTROLS ONE TWO-STATE VALVE. It selects the open command from the automatic source or, when the valve is in hand, from the operator; drops that command on any latched fault, on an external inhibit, or on loss of the system permissive; detects and latches a failure to open and a failure to close; condenses those and an external fault into one fault bit and two consequence-class bits; enables an upstream component once the valve is proven open; counts operations; publishes a status code; and writes a four-bit alarm word. THERE IS NO CLOSE COMMAND - the output dropping IS the close, and the valve fails shut with no energy on it. THE WHOLE CALLER-VISIBLE INTERFACE IS THE SINGLE STATIC IO of type UDT_Valve; the block declares no INPUT, OUTPUT or IN_OUT parameters, so the instance DB IS the interface - the caller writes into it and the panel binds to it. The call site therefore shows nothing of what was wired, and whoever calls this block must keep its writes to an instance's struct IMMEDIATELY ADJACENT to that instance's CALL rather than scattered. THE POSITION FEEDBACK IS A COMPUTED BOOL AND THE BLOCK DOES NOT KNOW WHAT PRODUCED IT: a real limit contact and an inference the caller draws from any process variable arrive on the same member, so thresholds, windows, magnitudes and attribution all live in whatever computes it and none of them is built in here. BOTH DETECTIONS FIRE ON POSITIVE EVIDENCE OF THE WRONG STATE - commanded open and the position says not open, commanded shut and the position says still open - and neither fires on the absence of evidence of the right one, so a quiet feedback is never read as a sealed valve. PositionValid carries the cannot-tell case: it gates whether a fault may arm and is never read as a position in either direction, so a valve nobody can judge raises neither fault. PositionConclusive carries a second and different gate - the verdict has had long enough to be decisive - and BOTH must be true before either detection arms. WHERE THE POSITION IS INFERRED, THE DETECTION WINDOW IS COMPUTED BY THE CALLING BLOCK AND ARRIVES ON PositionConclusive, so how long a fault took to appear cannot be answered from inside this block: the fail-to time here is a short confirmation on a settled verdict, and the period over which evidence was gathered belongs to whoever computed it. WHAT THIS BLOCK LEAVES TO ITS CALLER, each deliberately absent rather than missing: any interlock that reads a SIBLING device, which arrives through InhibitValve because a block cannot see its siblings; re-driving the valve to a required state after a power failure or a safety stop, which is a sequencing decision and not a valve decision; how it learns that its process is simulated; and the meaning of the suppressor cause it publishes. IO is retained in full - the whole struct, not only the latched causes - so a latched critical fault survives a power cycle; the alarm word and status code are rewritten every scan, so retaining them is a stale value for one scan and never a second seal-in.

Drives the valve's commanded state. The open request comes from the automatic source, or from the hand source while the valve is in hand - THE TWO SOURCES REPLACE EACH OTHER RATHER THAN COMBINING, so there is no state in which both partly drive the valve and no order of events that leaves the operator and the sequence disagreeing about who has it. That request must then pass an external inhibit, the block's OWN fault condensation, and the system-healthy permissive; any one of the three de-energises the valve whatever either source is asking for, and de-energising is the safe direction by construction - a device that has just reported it is not doing what it was told is not a device to keep driving. THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO SEAL-IN AND NO SECOND COMMAND BIT: a seal-in would sit outside the inhibit terms and defeat them, and a second bit would be identical to this one every scan. INTERLOCKS THAT READ SIBLING VALVES ARRIVE THROUGH InhibitValve, because a block cannot see its siblings. The fault bit read here is the previous scan's; the one-scan lag on closing is immaterial against any actuator travel time.
Valve Open / Close

Converts the two operator-facing times from Real SECONDS into the DInt millisecond presets the timers need: FTTime to FTTimeMS - ONE preset shared by both fail-to timers, so they are one setting and not two free to drift apart - then EnableUPSTime to EnableUPSTimeMS. Both conversions are kept here rather than repeated at each timer, so the times-a-thousand idiom is done once and visibly consistently. THE PAIRING IS BY INDEX, NOT BY ADJACENCY: every multiply renders in one contiguous run and every convert in the next, so the first convert takes the first multiply's result and the second takes the second's. They are not two independent pairs, and reordering the lines silently swaps the presets.
HMI Times

Normalises the position source into FBOpen, which is TRUE whenever the valve is PROVEN OPEN, whichever state the source is actually wired to prove. Which state that is is a WIRING FACT, and it is answered once, here, rather than being asserted in the name of every signal that carries it - so the opposite wiring costs a setting and not a code change, and there is one place to look when the answer turns out to have been wrong. Everything downstream reads FBOpen and never has to remember the sense.
Position Feedback, Normalised To Prove Open

Raises and latches the fail-to-open cause: the valve is commanded open, the position source is trustworthy, and it still says the valve is not open, continuously for longer than the fail-to time. IT FIRES ON POSITIVE EVIDENCE OF THE WRONG STATE and never on the absence of evidence of the right one. It is ARMED FROM A COMMAND THE PROGRAM ITSELF ISSUED - the valve was TOLD to change state, so the window in which its effect must appear starts from something certain, where arming from an inference would be one more thing that can be wrong. PositionValid is the cannot-tell case and it REMOVES the detection rather than degrading it: on a valve with no position source of any kind it is permanently false and this fault can never raise, which is the honest answer for a valve nobody can judge. THE SEAL-IN FOR THIS FACT IS HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE; the alarm bit downstream is a direct unlatched read of it.
Fail To Open

Raises and latches the fail-to-close cause: the valve is commanded shut, the position source is trustworthy, and it still says the valve is open, for longer than the fail-to time - the same preset the open direction uses. IT PROVES THE VALVE DID NOT CLOSE AND IT NEVER PROVES THAT IT DID. A quiet feedback is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence: the actuator could have stalled between limits, the seat could be holding on debris that will shift, the sensor could have failed low. So a valve nobody can currently judge leaves this fault QUIET rather than CLEAR, and telling those two apart at the panel is what the published suppressor cause exists for.
Fail To Close

Latches the external fault input into a cause bit of the block's own, held until reset, on the same seal-in shape as the two detections above. IT IS A SEPARATE BIT AND NOT A RESET COIL ON THE INPUT: latching the caller's own input in place would give that member two writers - the caller who raises it and this block which clears it - where a separate cause bit leaves it with one, and puts this fact's seal-in at a detection network like every other cause.
External Fault Latch

Condenses the three latched causes into the one fault bit the control logic and the owning caller read. A pure OR with NO SEAL-IN OF ITS OWN - every term is already sealed at its own detection network, and a second seal here would be a duplicate that could not be cleared with the cause. ITS POSITION UPSTREAM OF THE ALARM-WRITE NETWORK IS WHAT MAKES SUPPRESSION SAFE - the panel can be emptied and this bit cannot - and it is what the command rung reads for its fail-safe, so the valve closing itself on its own fault is not defeatable by suppression either. The standing in-hand indication is deliberately not a term.
Faults

Sets the critical-class consequence bit - drop outputs and freeze - for applications whose severity scheme separates a fault that must do that from one that need only freeze the step in progress. EXHAUSTIVELY: a failure to close on an instance configured as fail-close-critical, and nothing else, ever. MEMBERSHIP IS A PROPERTY OF THE INSTANCE AND NOT OF THE CONDITION, which is why the interface carries a configuration bit for it at all: the same physical condition - a valve still passing while shut - is a nuisance on one duty and a hazard on another, so the class is told to the block rather than inferred by it. Where that bit is clear this one is permanently clear, which is a TRUE STATEMENT ABOUT THAT INSTANCE and not a gap. Pure OR, no seal-in, upstream of every suppression term, so a suppressed critical fault still drops outputs.
Critical Class Consequence

Sets the error-class consequence bit - freeze the affected phase and inhibit the next step. The exact complement of the network above: a failure to open is the lesser class wherever it is detected, a failure to close is the lesser class only where it is not the greater one, and an external fault is the lesser class always. WHAT FEEDS NEITHER CLASS BIT: the in-hand indication, which is a deliberate act and must not freeze anything. Between them the two bits partition every latched cause with none left over, so the fault condensation above is identical to their OR on every instance.
Error Class Consequence

Publishes the standing indication that this valve is in hand, as a direct read of the mode bit. A STANDING CONDITION AND NOT A FAULT: no seal-in, no clearing on reset, and it feeds neither the fault condensation nor either consequence bit. The fact has exactly one home here, and the alarm word carries a view of it rather than a second copy.
Valve In Hand

Enables the component this valve feeds, once the valve has been proven open for the enable time. IT REQUIRES POSITIVE PROOF AND DOES NOT ASSUME IT - the valve must be commanded open AND the position source must say it is open - so a valve with no position source never enables; the failure mode being guarded is a downstream device starting into a shut valve. The block's own fault also drops the enable, so nothing it feeds keeps running on a valve that has reported itself faulty.
Valve Proven Open, Enable Upstream Component

Counts one operation each time this valve is proven open, and rolls over at the ceiling rather than saturating. The count runs off an explicitly constructed rising edge - the debounced proven-open state compared against its stored previous scan, then the stored copy updated - built out this way because neither the built-in edge instruction nor counter instructions are used here. THE TWO COILS MUST STAY IN THIS ORDER: the edge is computed from last scan's stored copy and the copy is updated after it, and swapping them gives an edge that never fires. THE DEBOUNCE IS A FIXED CONSTANT AND NOT A SETTING, deliberately - it exists only so a chattering position source cannot inflate a wear count, it is far shorter than any real actuator stroke, and making it tunable would invite its being tuned into a second fail-to time. At the ceiling the move to zero runs first and the add then takes the count to one on the same scan.
Valve Operation Counter

Writes the operator-facing status code for this valve: -1 faulted, 0 closed, 1 commanded open and travelling, 2 proven open. A CHAIN OF OVERRIDING MOVES EXECUTED IN LISTED ORDER, LAST ENABLED WINS, which is why the fault case is last and why adding a state is one line rather than a re-cut of a comparison tree. THERE IS NO SEPARATE IN-HAND CODE - two covers proven open whether it was reached by hand or by the automatic source, because the in-hand fact is published on its own bit and a status code that also carried it would force every reader to decode a combination.
Valve Status Telemetry

Writes the whole of this valve's alarm word, and no other network writes any bit of it. EVERY BIT IS A DIRECT, UNLATCHED READ of a cause already latched at its own detection network, ANDed with that bit's suppressor where it has one - the alarm INHERITS latched behaviour by reading a latched bit and does not implement it, so there is no seal-in anywhere in this network. THE SUPPRESSOR AND-TERMS ARE THE ONLY PLACE SUPPRESSION REACHES. Control reads FaultActive, which is written upstream, so filtering changes WHAT THE OPERATOR IS SHOWN and can never change WHAT THE PLANT DOES - a suppressed fault still closes this valve and still holds whatever the caller holds. THE BIT MAP: %X0 = FTO = <Valve> - failed to open - check the valve, its supply and the equipment that moves it. %X1 = FTC = <Valve> - still open when commanded shut - check the actuator and the seat; where two valves are separated by magnitude alone the site text must also carry the known misattribution, because a leak too small for the more severe threshold is reported against the less severe valve. %X2 = ExtFault = <Valve> - external actuator fault - check the actuator's own diagnostics. %X3 = OverrideActive = <Valve> - in hand - no action, released at the panel. BITS 4, 5 AND 6 ARE WRITTEN BY NO NETWORK IN THIS BLOCK and bits 7 to 15 are spare: this block writes only the four conditions it detects, and an application allocates the rest. NEITHER ExtFault NOR OverrideActive HAS A SUPPRESSOR TERM, and there is no input to give them one: the external fault is detected outside this block by something that already knows its own evidence, and the in-hand indication is itself commonly a suppressor of other alarms, so it must not be capable of being hidden.
Valve Alarm Word
